question: ATS 7.25 checks fiber length, breaks, and splices primarily with:
choices: A megohmmeter
An optical time-domain reflectometer
A DLRO
A primary-injection set
explanation: The optical tests are OTDR for length, fractures, and splice reflections, plus a power-loss set for attenuation. A megger does not see a cracked strand.

question: Visible bends in a fiber run are acceptable when they are:
choices: Tighter than the trunking will allow
Not less than the manufacturer’s minimum bend radius
At least 1 inch, for every cable
Ignored if the link still passes light
explanation: 7.25 holds bends to the manufacturer’s minimum radius. A link that still “has light” can be bruised enough to fail the loss spec later.

question: With no project loss spec, fiber attenuation is held to:
choices: 1 dB per splice, always
The manufacturer’s recommendation, reported in dB/km
Table 100.1 megohms
Whatever the OTDR defaults to
explanation: 7.25.D.3 says attenuation is expressed in dB/km and, when the site has no spec, losses stay within the manufacturer’s recommendation. Inventing 1 dB is not that paragraph.

question: Which statement is not a valid description of an ATS fiber test?
choices: Length, breaks, and splices are checked optically
Attenuation is compared with the project spec or the manufacturer
The strand is hipot-tested at the power-cable VLF voltage
Bend radius follows the manufacturer
explanation: Fiber is not a power conductor and it is not meggered or hipotted like XLPE. An optical test finds length and splices. Calling hipot an advantage of fiber is the wrong test.

question: Connector and splice loss on a new fiber run is measured with an optical power loss test set. From where?
choices: From one end only
From both ends of the cable
At the midpoint splice
From the OTDR end only
explanation: ATS has the connector and splice loss measured from both ends of the cable with an optical loss test set. Fiber loss can differ by direction, so one end is not enough. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.B.4.

question: On a relay fiber link, the transmit and receive power readings at the local and remote devices are judged against:
choices: The manufacturer's published data
A fixed 3 dB limit
The cable's bend radius
The OTDR trace length
explanation: ATS has you measure transmit and receive power at both devices and compare the results to the manufacturer's published data. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.B.5 and D.5.

question: How do you spot an excessive splice loss on an OTDR result?
choices: By reading the reflected power versus distance graph
By the meter's pass/fail lamp only
By measuring insulation resistance of the jacket
By the cable's printed footage marks
explanation: ATS says the OTDR signal is analyzed for backscatter and for excessive connection or splice loss by viewing the reflected power against distance graph. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.D.1 and D.2.

question: A 3.2 km fiber link shows 1.6 dB of total attenuation. Expressed the way ATS 7.25 reports it, that's:
choices: 0.2 dB/km
0.5 dB/km
2.0 dB/km
5.1 dB/km
explanation: 1.6 dB / 3.2 km = 0.5 dB/km. That figure is then compared with the project spec or the manufacturer's recommendation. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.B.3 and D.3.

question: Which of these is NOT an advantage of fiber over copper for a relay communications link?
choices: It isn't affected by electromagnetic interference
It doesn't carry ground-loop currents between locations
It carries more information over longer distances
It tolerates tighter bends and rougher handling than copper
explanation: Glass carries light, not current, so it ignores electrical noise and breaks ground loops between buildings, and it moves more information farther than copper. Toughness isn't one of its advantages: every fiber has a manufacturer minimum bend radius, and a tight bend adds loss even when some light still gets through. Source: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 1 and ch. 5; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.A.4.
reference: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 1 and ch. 5; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.25.A.4

question: A relay in the switchyard talks to a relay in the control house over fiber instead of copper. The main electrical reason is:
choices: Fiber always costs less per foot than copper
Fiber gives electrical isolation and immunity to electrical noise, so ground loops and induced noise don't reach the relay
Fiber needs no connectors or splices
Fiber carries the remote relay's control power
explanation: Fiber is a dielectric. It makes no metallic path between the yard and the house, so it isolates the two ends from ground loops, and electromagnetic interference doesn't affect it. Noise immunity is often the main reason industrial and utility sites choose it. Cost depends on the job, fiber still needs connectors or splices, and it carries no useful power. Source: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 1 and ch. 5.
reference: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 1 and ch. 5

question: A fiber patch cord has a yellow jacket and is printed 9/125. What kind of fiber is it?
choices: Multimode with a 62.5 µm core
Singlemode, with a core of about 9 µm in 125 µm cladding
Laser-optimized multimode (OM3)
Plastic optical fiber
explanation: Under the TIA-598 color code, multimode jackets are traditionally orange (OM3 is aqua) and singlemode jackets are yellow. Singlemode cores are about 8 to 10 µm, small enough that light travels in a single path, which gives the longest reach and highest bandwidth. Multimode cores are 50 or 62.5 µm. Both use 125 µm cladding. Source: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 5 (fiber primer; color codes).
reference: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 5 (fiber primer; color codes)

question: Graded-index multimode fiber was developed to fix what limitation of step-index multimode fiber?
choices: Dispersion from light taking different path lengths through the core, which limits bandwidth
Too little attenuation
Brittle plastic cores
The need for a laser source
explanation: A step-index core is one uniform material, so light on longer zigzag paths arrives later than light on short paths, pulses smear, and bandwidth stays low. Graded-index cores vary the glass composition so the longer paths are compensated, giving hundreds of times more bandwidth. Singlemode goes further by allowing only one path. Source: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 5 (fiber primer).
reference: FOA Reference Guide to Premises Cabling (J. Hayes), ch. 5 (fiber primer)
